extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of mineralogy/crystallography (geology/mineralogy students and researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Describing and classifying crystals in the hexagonal system (rhombohedral and hexagonal divisions), including symmetry-classes, characteristic forms, axial representations, twinning, growth irregularities, theories of crystal structure, and directional physical properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Hexagonal System
rubrics_metrics.description: Crystals of this system are characterized by the presence of a single axis of either triad or hexad symmetry (the 'principal' or 'morphological' axis); those with a triad axis form the rhombohedral/trigonal division, and those with a hexad axis the hexagonal division. Rhombohedral and hexagonal divisions may be treated separately or related (hemihedral relationships, combinations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that owing to the single triad/hexad axis, crystallographic axes of reference differ from the five other systems; two axial representation methods are in common use (rhombohedral axes for rhombohedral division, hexagonal axes for hexagonal division), and sometimes either set is used in both divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhombohedral axes (axial representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhombohedral axes are taken parallel to the three sets of edges of a rhombohedron: they are inclined to one another at equal oblique angles, equally inclined to the principal axis, all of equal length and interchangeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With such axes there is no axial ratio to state; an angle between the axes (the rhombohedral angle) or an angle between face normal and the principal axis may be given as a constant for the substance (example: calcite rhombohedral angle 74°55' or face-normal to principal axis 44°36½').

rubrics_metrics.name: Hexagonal axes (axial representation) and plane indices
rubrics_metrics.description: Hexagonal axes: four axes — one vertical principal axis (c) and three horizontal axes (a) in a plane at 60° to one another. The three horizontal axes are equal in length (a) while the vertical is different (c). Plane indices are four-number symbols {hikl} with h + i + k = 0 for the horizontal indices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The axial ratio a:c is characteristic for a substance (examples: beryl a:c = 1 : 0.4989 often written c = 0.4989; zinc c = 1.3564). Horizontal axes may be taken parallel or perpendicular to prism faces or bipyramid edges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holosymmetric class (rhombohedral; ditrigonal scalenohedral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Triad axis with three similar planes of symmetry inclined at 60° intersecting in the triad; three similar dyad axes each perpendicular to a plane of symmetry; a centre of symmetry. Seven simple forms occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple forms include rhombohedron ({100}, and in general {hkk}), scalenohedron ({hkl}, e.g. {201'}) with direct and inverse sets, hexagonal bipyramid ({_hkl_} where h - 2k + l = 0), hexagonal prisms (first and second order), dihexagonal prism, basal pinacoid {111}. Examples of substances: calcite, corundum (ruby, sapphire), haematite, ice, sodium nitrate, thymol, elements such as arsenic, antimony, bismuth, selenium, tellurium, graphite (perhaps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhombohedron (form) and variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhombohedron consists of six rhomb-shaped faces with edges equal; there are direct and inverse sets related by rotation about the principal axis. Fundamental rhombohedron indices {100}; other rhombohedra {211}, {41'1'}, {110}, {221'}, {111'}, generally {hkk}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhombohedra's faces are perpendicular to planes of symmetry; relations between forms and indices are best studied with stereographic projection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalenohedron (form) and relation to rhombohedron
rubrics_metrics.description: Scalenohedron is bounded by twelve scalene triangles; general indices {hkl}. Its lateral edges coincide with those of an inscribed rhombohedron; e.g., inscribed rhombohedron {100} → scalenohedron {201'} (characteristic of calcite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Has direct and inverse sets; angles of face edges differ and orientation/indices can differ even if similar in form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hexagonal bipyramid (form) in rhombohedral classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Bounded by twelve isosceles triangles; indices {210}, {412'}, general form (_hkl_) where h - 2k + l = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be considered in relation to scalenohedron/rhombohedron forms; indices follow the h - 2k + l = 0 condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ditrigonal pyramidal class (rhombohedral; hemimorphic-hemihedral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three similar planes of symmetry intersect in the triad axis; there are no dyad axes and no centre of symmetry. The triad axis is uniterminal and polar, so crystals are differently developed at the two ends and are pyro-electric. Forms are all open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple forms include trigonal pyramid {hkk}, ditrigonal pyramid {hkl}, hexagonal pyramid (hkl) with h - 2k + l = 0, trigonal prism {21'1'} / {2'11}, hexagonal prism {101'}, ditrigonal prism {hk'l'} (h + k + l = 0), basal pedion (111) or (1'1'1'). Examples: tourmaline, pyrargyrite, proustite, iodyrite, greenockite, zincite, spangolite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trapezohedral class (rhombohedral; trapezohedral-hemihedral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three similar dyad axes inclined 60° to one another and perpendicular to the triad axis; no planes or centre of symmetry. Dyad axes are uniterminal and pyro-electric axes. Many crystals of this class rotate the plane of polarization of transmitted light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms include trigonal trapezohedron {hkl} and trigonal bipyramid {hkl} with condition h - 2k + l = 0. Examples: quartz and cinnabar (which rotate plane-polarized light), certain dithionates and organic compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhombohedral class (rhombohedral; parallel-faced hemihedral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only symmetry elements are the triad axis and a centre of symmetry. General form {hkl} is a rhombohedron and is a hemihedral form of the scalenohedron; {hkl} with h - 2k + l = 0 is hemihedral of hexagonal bipyramid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other forms (rhombohedra hkk, hexagonal prisms {21'1'} and {101'}, basal pinacoid {111}) are geometrically same as in holosymmetric class. Examples: phenacite, dioptase, willemite, dolomite, ilmenite, pyrophanite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonal pyramidal class (rhombohedral; hemimorphic-tetartohedral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the triad axis of symmetry, which is uniterminal; the general form {hkl} is a trigonal pyramid consisting of three faces at one end of the crystal. Prisms are trigonal prisms and perpendicular to these are two pedions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very rare class: sodium periodate (NaIO4.3H2O) is cited and its crystals are circularly polarizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonal bipyramidal class (rhombohedral)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a plane of symmetry perpendicular to the triad axis. Trigonal pyramids of the previous class become trigonal bipyramids; prisms are trigonal prisms; basal pinacoid parallel to the plane of symmetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No natural example known in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ditrigonal bipyramidal class (rhombohedral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three similar planes of symmetry intersecting in the triad axis and a fourth plane of symmetry perpendicular to them; three similar dyad axes at intersection; no centre of symmetry. General form bounded by twelve scalene triangles; two sets of indices {hkl, p'q'r'} for faces above and below equatorial plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hexagonal bipyramids, hexagonal prism {101'} and basal pinacoid {111} geometrically similar to holosymmetric class. Example mineral: benitoite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holosymmetric class (hexagonal division; dihexagonal bipyramidal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hexad axis with six planes of symmetry of two kinds intersecting in it and an equatorial plane of symmetry; six dyad axes of two kinds perpendicular to vertical planes. Seven simple forms occur for the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms include dihexagonal bipyramid {hikl} (24 scalene triangles), hexagonal bipyramids (first and second order) with indices like {101'1} and {112'1}, dihexagonal prism {hiko}, hexagonal prisms of first {1010} and second order {112'0}, basal pinacoid {0001}. Examples: beryl (emerald), connellite, zinc, magnesium and beryllium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bipyramidal class (hexagonal division; parallel-faced hemihedral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plane of symmetry perpendicular to hexad axis and a centre of symmetry are present. Closed forms are hexagonal bipyramids; open forms are hexagonal prisms or basal pinacoid. General form {hikl} is hemihedral with parallel faces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example minerals: apatite, pyromorphite, mimetite, vanadinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dihexagonal pyramidal class (hexagonal division; hemimorphic-hemihedral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Six planes of symmetry of two kinds intersect in the hexad axis which is uniterminal; all forms are open. General form {hikl} is a dihexagonal pyramid (twelve faces at one end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hexagonal pyramids {hoh'l} and (h.h.2'h'.l) consist of six faces at one end; prisms geometrically same as in holosymmetric class. Examples (possibly placed here but may belong to rhombohedral): iodyrite (AgI), greenockite (CdS), wurtzite (ZnS), zincite (ZnO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trapezohedral class (hexagonal division; trapezohedral-hemihedral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Six dyad axes of two kinds perpendicular to the hexad axis; general form is the hexagonal trapezohedron bounded by twelve trapezoidal faces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other simple forms are geometrically same as in holosymmetric class. Examples: certain salts (barium-antimonyl dextro-tartrate + potassium nitrate and corresponding lead salt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hexagonal pyramidal class (hexagonal division; hemimorphic-tetartohedral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the hexad axis is associated (uniterminal); pyramids consist of six faces at one end of the crystal, and prisms are hexagonal prisms. Pedions are perpendicular to the hexad axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: lithium potassium sulphate, strontium-antimonyl dextro-tartrate, lead-antimonyl dextro-tartrate, nepheline (placed here due to absence of symmetry in etched prism faces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular grouping of crystals and special aggregate structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Crystals of the same kind may group in parallel positions producing dendritic/branch-like aggregations or fibrous structures. Aggregation and interference between crystals produce special external shapes characteristic of some substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: dendritic native copper or magnetite, sceptre-quartz (continued growth with different external form/colour). Regular intergrowths of different substances occur with certain planes/edges parallel (reference given to literature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and elements of twinning (twin-plane and twin-axis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twinning: two crystals (individuals of same kind) grown together symmetrically such that one portion can be brought into the position of the other by reflection across a plane or rotation about an axis. Twin-plane is parallel to one of the faces or a possible face; twin-axis is parallel to an edge or perpendicular to a face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: gypsum twinned on plane (100); octahedron twinned on face (111) relates to spinel twin-law. Composition-plane of union may coincide with twin-plane (juxtaposition-twins) or not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of twinning and recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Juxtaposition-twins: composition surface coincides with twin-plane. Interpenetration twins: one crystal rotated into the other (example: cubes twinned via rotation about triad axis or reflection across octahedral plane). Hemitrope: rotation through two right angles (introduced by Hauy). Symmetric twins explained only by reflection. Recognition often by re-entrant angles but not always (e.g., quartz may show no re-entrant angles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polysynthetic twinning = repeated twinning on same plane producing laminated structures and planes of parting; lamellar twinning can be produced artificially by pressure (e.g. calcite, glide-plane). Mimetic or pseudo-symmetric twins produce apparent higher symmetry (pseudo-hexagonal, pseudo-cubic), explaining many optical anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregularities of growth and 'habit' of crystals
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual crystals often deviate from ideal symmetrical forms because of uneven deposition during growth (attachment, differing supply of material). Habit (actual external shape) varies widely for same substance depending on growth conditions (fused mass vs solutions, solvents, temperature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: misshapen octahedra (elongated or flattened) still retain crystallographic directions and angles; cuprite variety chalcotrichite forms matted hairs (elongated individuals). Calcite shows wide variety of habits but referable to same fundamental form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallites, microlites and early arrested growth forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Incipient crystals with arrested development are called crystallites (found in imperfectly crystallized substances and glassy rocks). At more advanced stage such bodies (microlites) react on polarized light and are minute rods, needles, or hairs aggregated into feathery/spherulitic forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names: globulites, margarites, longulites (Vogelsang). Microlites are common constituents of microcrystalline igneous rocks and as inclusions in larger crystals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusions, cavities and 'negative crystals'
rubrics_metrics.description: Crystals often contain inclusions of foreign matter (other minerals, liquids, gases). Cavities may have rounded boundaries or shapes matching the surrounding crystal ('negative crystals').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusions can be substantial (e.g., calcite containing up to 60% included sand); cavities may enclose liquids with movable gas bubbles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of crystal faces: striae, vicinal faces, prerosion faces, drusy and twisted surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Faces are rarely perfectly plane; commonly they are striated, studded, pitted, cavernous, curved or twisted. Striae are parallel grooves/furrows from oscillatory combination between adjacent faces. Vicinal faces are smooth bright surfaces slightly inclined from true face position (indices only expressible with very high numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Striae directions are characteristic: e.g., quartz prism faces striated horizontally, beryl vertically; cubes of pyrites striated parallel to an edge, cubes of blende striated parallel to a diagonal. Vicinal faces formed during growth, prerosion faces and minute etched faces can cause deviations in measured angles. Pitting/cavities may result from rapid growth; twisted surfaces often built from smaller crystals; drusy surfaces are formed by replacement of faces with small faces of other forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicinal faces and their measurement implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Vicinal faces are nearly parallel smooth faces inclined only a few minutes of arc from true face; their indices can only be expressed by very high numbers, and their presence causes measured angles to deviate slightly from true angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in alum the octahedral face (111) is often replaced by very low triakis-octahedra such as (251.251.250), studied by H. A. Miers (Phil. Trans. 1903). Vicinal faces formed during growth; other high-index faces may be formed by corrosion subsequent to growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theories of crystal structure: aims and twofold problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Ultimate aim is to determine internal structure of crystals from physical and chemical data. Problem is twofold: (1) formulate a theory for disposition of molecules that conforms with observed symmetry (mathematical problem); (2) determine orientation of atoms (or groups) composing molecules relative to crystal axes (requires knowledge of atomic/molecular structure). Considerations include polymorphism and relations of chemical structure to habit (isomorphism, morphotropy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References Part III for chemical-structure relations; cites historical approaches (Hauy, Bravais, Sohncke, Fedorov, Schoenflies, Barlow) and literature references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hauy's theory / space-lattice concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Hauy conceived a crystal as composed of elements bounded by cleavage planes arranged contiguously along parallel lines. Modern replacement: matter is not continuous; particles are equidistantly distributed along parallel lines forming a 'space-lattice' of three sets of parallel planes enclosing parallelepipeds with molecules at corners; permanence of form due to equilibrium of intermolecular/interatomic forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conceptual change retains the reticulated/net structure without continuity of matter; used as a basis for geometrical theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bravais lattices, Frankenheim and the count of systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Frankenheim (1835) determined fifteen partitionings of space; Bravais (1850) proved the identity/coalescence of some forms to leave fourteen lattices corresponding to seven distinct crystal systems and fourteen classes of symmetry (initially representing holohedral forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bravais' work explained holohedral forms but left hemihedral/tetartohedral classes to be treated by additional assumptions about differences in symmetry of crystal elements (e.g., polar differences along members of the lattice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sohncke point-systems and completion of symmetry classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Sohncke (1879) developed the idea of regular point-systems (identical arrangements of molecular points) and derived sixty-five such arrangements; these can be obtained from Bravais lattices by interpenetrating lattices under homogeneity conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further work by Fedorov, Schoenflies and Barlow (1890-1894) showed how Sohncke's theory, with mirror-image considerations, explained the full thirty-two classes of crystal symmetry and 230 distinct types of crystal structure (space groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elasticity and cohesion in crystals (directional dependence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many physical properties of crystals vary with direction; elastic constants must be determined on bars/plates cut with known orientations. The 'elasticity surface' expressing coefficients in various directions has configuration symmetrical with the crystal's symmetry planes/axes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in calcite the elasticity surface is roughly a rounded rhombohedron symmetrical about three vertical planes. Homogeneous elastic deformation (pressure on all sides) produces effects similar to temperature change; surfaces expressing compression coefficients have higher symmetry (sphere, spheroid or ellipsoid). Beyond elastic limits, permanent deformation occurs as plastic deformation (particles displaced without change in orientation) or breakage along cleavage surfaces or irregular fracture.
